'''''Nuphar lutea''''', the '''yellow water-lily''', is an [[aquatic plant]] of the family [[Nymphaeaceae]], native to northern temperate and some subtropical regions of [[Europe]], northwest [[Africa]], and western [[Asia]].<ref>Flora Europaea: [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Nuphar&SPECIES_XREF=lutea&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Nuphar lutea'']</ref><ref>{{GRIN | access-date = 17 December 2017}}</ref> This species was used as a food source and in medicinal practices from prehistoric times with potential research and medical applications going forward.<ref name=MonographGenusNuphar>{{cite thesis |last=Padgett |first=Donald Jay |date=1997 |title=A Biosystematic Monograph of the Genus ''Nuphar'' Sm. (Nymphaeaceae) |type=Doctoral Dissertation |publisher=University of New Hampshire Scholars' Repository |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/215520528.pdf  |access-date=21 December 2020}}</ref>{{rp|30}}

== Description ==
===Vegetative characteristics===
''Nuphar lutea'' is an aquatic, rhizomatous,<ref name = "Danin & Fragman-Sapir">Danin, A., & Fragman-Sapir, O. (n.d.). ''Nuphar lutea'' (L.) Sm. Flora of Israel and Adjacent Areas. Retrieved 5 December 2024, from https://flora.org.il/en/plants/NUPLUT/</ref> perennial herb with stout,<ref name = "Flora of China">''Nuphar lutea'' (Linnaeus) Smith. (n.d.). Flora of China @ efloras.org. Retrieved 5 December 2024, from http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=220009308</ref> branching, spongy, 3–8(–15) cm wide rhizomes.<ref name = "Padgett" /> It has floating and submerged leaves.<ref name = "Janßen" /><ref name = "Padgett">Padgett, D. J. (2007). A Monograph of ''Nuphar'' (Nymphaeaceae). Rhodora, 109(937), 1–95. http://www.jstor.org/stable/23314744</ref> The broadly elliptic to ovate,<ref name = "Padgett" /> green,<ref name = "Padgett" /> leathery floating leaf<ref name = "Flora of China" /> with an entire margin, a deep sinus and spreading basal lobes<ref name = "Flora of China" /> is 16–30 cm long, and 11.5–22.1 cm wide.<ref name = "Padgett" /> The adaxial surface is glabrous, and the abaxial surface is glabrous or pubescent.<ref name = "Flora of China" /> The trigonous petiole is 3–10 mm wide.<ref name = "Padgett" /> The very thin submerged leaf with undulate margins has short petioles.<ref name = "Janßen" />

===Generative characteristics===
The fragrant,<ref name = "Lüder, 2008">Lüder, R. (2008). Grundkurs Pflanzenbestimmung: Eine Praxisanleitung für Anfänger und Fortgeschrittene (4th ed.). p. 118. Quelle & Meyer Verlag.</ref> solitary, yellow, subglobose, 30–65 mm wide, floating<ref name = "Janßen">Janßen, D. (n.d.). Gelbe Teichrose Nuphar lutea (L.) Sm. Flora Emslandia - Pflanzen Im Emsland. Retrieved 5 December 2024, from http://www.flora-emslandia.de/wildblumen/nymphaeaceae/nuphar/nuphar_lutea.htm</ref> or emergent flowers have 4–10 mm wide, glabrous to pubescent peduncles.<ref name = "Padgett" /> The 5(–6)<ref name = "Padgett" /> yellow, broadly ovate to orbicular sepals<ref name = "Flora of China" /> with a rounded apex are 2–3 cm long.<ref name = "Flora of China" /> The 11–20 obovate inconspicuous petals with a rounded apex are 7.5–23 mm long. The androecium consists of numerous stamens with 4–7 mm long, yellow anthers.<ref name = "Padgett" /> The sulcate, spheroidal pollen grains are 26–50 μm long.<ref name = "Halbritter & Svojtka, 2016">Halbritter H., Svojtka M. 2016. ''Nuphar lutea''. In: PalDat - A palynological database. https://www.paldat.org/pub/Nuphar_lutea/302325; accessed 2024-12-05</ref> The gynoecium consists of 5-20 carpels. The stigmatic disk with an entire margin is 7–19 mm wide.<ref name = "Flora of China" /> The urceolate, green, 2.6–4.5 cm long, and 1.9–3.4 cm wide fruit,<ref name = "Padgett" /> which is enclosed in persistent sepals,<ref name = "Janßen" /> bears up to 400 ovoid,<ref name = "Padgett" /> olive green,<ref name = "Padgett" /><ref name = "Flora of China" /> 3.5–5 mm long, and 3.5 mm wide seeds.<ref name = "Padgett" />

===Cytology===
The chromosome count is 2n = 34.<ref name = "Flora of China" />

== Taxonomy ==
It was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] as ''Nymphaea lutea'' L. in 1753. Later, it was transferred to genus ''Nuphar'' Sm. as ''Nuphar lutea'' (L.) Sm. by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in 1809.<ref name = "POWO" /> It is the type species of its genus.<ref name = "Tropicos a">Missouri Botanical Garden. (n.d.-ae). ''Nuphar'' Sm. Tropicos. Retrieved 3 March 2025, from https://www.tropicos.org/name/40029474</ref> It is placed in the section [[Nuphar sect. Nuphar|''Nuphar'' sect. ''Nuphar'']].<ref name = "GRIN">USDA, Agricultural Research Service, National Plant Germplasm System. 2025. Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN Taxonomy). National Germplasm Resources Laboratory, Beltsville, Maryland. URL: https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomydetail?id=416165. Accessed 3 March 2025.</ref>

===Species delimitation===
Some botanists have treated ''Nuphar lutea'' as the sole species in ''Nuphar'', including all the other species in it as [[subspecies]] and giving the species a [[holarctic]] range,<ref>Beal, E. O. (1956). Taxonomic revision of the genus ''Nuphar'' Sm. of North America and Europe. ''Journal of the Elisha Mitchell Scientific Society'' 72: 317–346.</ref><ref name="nrcs">{{cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=NULU |title=Plants Profile: ''Nuphar lutea'' |work=Natural Resources Conservation Service |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=13 April 2010}}</ref> but the genus is now more usually divided into 8–15 species (see ''[[Nuphar]]'' for details).<ref name="POWOgenus">{{cite web | title=''Nuphar'' Sm. | website=Plants of the World Online | date=2020-07-17 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:331808-2 | access-date=2026-01-03}}</ref><ref>USDA Germplasm Resources Information Network: [http://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/npgs/html/genus.pl?8319 ''Nuphar''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090827124155/http://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/npgs/html/genus.pl?8319 |date=2009-08-27 }}</ref>

===Etymology===
The specific epithet ''lutea'', from the Latin ''luteus'', means deep yellow or golden yellow.<ref>{{cite book | last=Stearn | first=William Thomas | title=Botanical Latin | publisher=David & Charles | publication-place=Newton Abbot, Devon; North Pomfret, Vt | date=1983 | isbn=0-7153-8548-8 | page=460}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
===Habitat===
Habitat for ''Nuphar lutea'' ranges widely from moving to stagnant waters of "shallow lakes, ponds, swamps, river and stream margins, canals, ditches, and tidal reaches of freshwater streams"; alkaline to acidic waters; and sea level to mountainous lakes up to 3,000 metres in altitude.<ref name=MonographGenusNuphar/>{{rp|24}} The species is less tolerant of water pollution than water-lilies in the genus ''[[Nymphaea]]''.<ref name=blamey/> This [[aquatic plant]] grows in shallow water and [[wetlands]], with its roots in the sediment and its leaves floating on the water surface; it can grow in water up to 5 metres deep.<ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref> It is usually found in shallower water than the [[Nymphaea alba|white water-lily]], and often in beaver ponds. Since the flooded soils are deficient in oxygen, [[aerenchyma]] in the leaves and rhizome transport oxygen from the atmosphere to the rhizome roots. Often there is mass flow from the young leaves into the rhizome, and out through the older leaves.<ref>Dacey, J. W. H. (1981). Pressurized ventilation in the yellow water lily. Ecology, 62, 1137–47.</ref> This "ventilation mechanism" has become the subject of research because of this species' substantial benefit to the surrounding ecosystem by "exhaling" [[methane gas]] from lake sediments.<ref name=MethaneEfflux>{{cite journal |last1=Dacey |first1=J. W. H. |last2=Klug |first2=M. J. |date=March 23, 1979 |title=Methane Efflux from Lake Sediments Through Water Lilies |journal=Science |volume=203 |issue=4386 |pages=1253–1255 |doi=10.1126/science.203.4386.1253|pmid=17841139 |bibcode=1979Sci...203.1253D |s2cid=8478786 }}</ref>

===Herbivory===
''Nuphar lutea'' plant colonies in turn are affected by organisms that eat its leaves, stems, and roots, including birds, deer, [[Eurasian elk|elk]], and more.<ref name=MonographGenusNuphar/>{{rp|27–29}} The water-lily leaf beetle, ''[[Galerucella nymphaeae]]'', spends its entire life cycle around various ''Nuphar'' species, exposing leaf tissue to microbial attack and loss of floating ability.<ref name=Water-lilyBeetle>{{cite journal |last=Kouki |first=Jari |date=December 1991 |title=The Effect of the Water-lily Beetle, Garerucella nymphaeae, on Leaf Production and Leaf Longevity of the Yellow Water-lily, Nuphar lutea |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1365-2427.1991.tb01402.x |journal=Freshwater Biology |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=347–353 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2427.1991.tb01402.x |access-date=23 December 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

As with other species in the order Nymphaeales, ''Nuphar lutea'' provides habitat for fish and a wide range of aquatic invertebrates, insects, snails, birds, crayfish, deer, and [[Eurasian beaver|beaver]] in shallow waters along lake, pond, and stream margins.<ref name=Nymphaeales>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Nymphaeales |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Life Sciences |date=26 February 2003 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons <!-- |id=www.els.net -->}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Nuphar lutea'' is native to the region spanning from Europe to Siberia, Xinjiang, China, and  North Algeria. It is extinct in Sicily, Italy. It has been introduced to Bangladesh, New Zealand, and the Russian region Primorye.<ref name = "POWO" />

== Conservation status ==
The [[IUCN]] conservation status is Least Concern (LC).<ref name = "IUCN" />

==Uses==
===Horticulture===
It is cultivated as an ornamental plant.<ref name = "EPPO">''Nuphar lutea''. (n.d.). EPPO Global Database. Retrieved 5 December 2024, from https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/NUPLU</ref>

===Food===
''Nuphar lutea'' is used as food.<ref name=Archaeobotany>{{cite book |last1=Vanhanen |first1=Santeri |last2=Lagerås |first2=Per |date=2020 |title=Archaeobotanical Studies of Past Plant Cultivation in Northern Europe |url=http://www.archaeobotany.eu |location=Kooiweg, Holland |publisher=Barkhuis |page=109 |isbn=9789493194113}}</ref>

=== Symbolism ===
Stylised red leaves of the yellow water-lily, known as ''[[seeblatt]]s'' or ''pompeblêden'' are used as a symbol of [[Frisia]]. The [[Flag of Friesland|flag of the Dutch province of Friesland]] features seven ''pompeblêden''.
[[Stone masons]] carved forms of the flowers on the [[Boss (architecture)|roof bosses]] of [[Bristol Cathedral]] and [[Westminster Abbey]], these are thought to encourage [[celibacy]].<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=29 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=9780276002175}}</ref>
